articles.title: Digger review – Tom Cruise’s loudmouth oil tycoon goes hard in Alejandro G Iñárritu’s eco-satire
articles.summary: One man’s irresponsible drilling causes a global crisis in Iñárritu’s exasperatingly laborious, self-congratulatory film. A new movie from the Oscar-winning Mexican director Alejandro González Iñárritu is always an event.
body: An ageing, paunchy Texan oil tycoon called “Digger” Rockwell is seen fretfully getting up in the morning, cooing over his horrible old incontinent cat, taking urgent messages from underlings about a certain situation developing in his drilling station in the frozen Arctic. He is played by Tom Cruise with a wispy baldingness and various other prostheses, together with a good-ol’-boy twang and a Stetson borrowed from Slim Pickens’s bomb-riding army major in Kubrick’s Dr Strangelove. His prized possession is the battered old shovel his granddaddy used a century before, digging for black gold as a penniless young man in the lone star state. Digger likes to brandish this to make a point.

Digger’s – and the world’s – troubles come to a head when he is informed by his cringingly polite, querulous and terrified chief scientist Ganesh (Riz Ahmed) that the company’s irresponsible drilling practices, of which Ganesh has been warning Digger for quite some time, have caused a crisis: a vast ice floe, many times the size of Manhattan island, has broken away from the Arctic landmass and is now moving quickly towards the coast of Norway. Its imminent landfall is going to be like a nuclear attack.
points: One man’s irresponsible drilling causes a global crisis in Iñárritu’s exasperatingly laborious, self-congratulatory film.

articles.title: Variety and Outfront Announce Experience and Culture Summit: The IRL Advantage, Featuring Questlove, Charlamagne tha God and Ice-T
articles.summary: Variety and Outfront today announced the first-ever Variety Experience and Culture Summit: The IRL Advantage presented by Outfront, taking place Oct. 7 in New York at The Penn District by Skylight.
body: “Partnering with Outfront on this first-ever summit reflects exactly the conversation the industry needs to be having right now,” said Michelle Fine-Smith, SVP, Global B2B Partnerships, Variety. “The leaders joining us, from CMOs rethinking brand experience to entertainers and sports icons building lifelong fandom, will explore why the IRL advantage, real-world connection, has become something that can’t be automated. There’s no better place to have that conversation than New York, a city that just celebrated a historic Knicks championship.”

“There’s a lot of talk about what in real-life (IRL) media means, but there’s no one-size-fits-all formula for breaking through to the audiences that matter most,” said Julie Massoni, Head of Enterprise Sales, West Coast, Outfront. “For an entertainment industry changing this quickly, IRL media is how you meet that disruption head-on — whether you’re driving attention to a series, a theatrical release, a concert, a festival or a sporting event, or you’re a brand trying to reach fans through them. This summit is about real examples of real-world campaigns that delivered real results.”

articles.title: Berlanti Productions Promotes Liam Driscoll to Creative Executive (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: Berlanti Productions has promoted Liam Driscoll to the role of creative executive, Variety has learned exclusively. Driscoll began his time at Berlanti Productions as Greg Berlanti’s assistant but will now be working across both film and TV.
body: “This is such an exciting time to be at the company,” Driscoll said. “There could be no better education in this business than working for Greg and Sarah. Their integrity and fierce advocacy for creatives is something I learn from each day. It’s a dream to work across projects that champion new exciting voices, while at the same time helping build the kind of classic shows and films that made me fall in love with this industry in the first place.”

Berlanti Productions is currently under an overall TV deal at Warner Bros. Television, where the company has been based for the past 15 years. Their current slates includes upcoming shows like “Afterlife with Archie” at Disney+, “Scooby-Doo: Origins” at Netflix, “How to Survive Without Me” at HBO Max, and “Stillwater” at Amazon Prime Video.

articles.title: Graham Norton Shoots Down ‘Conspiracy Theory’ That Taylor Swift’s ‘Opalite’ Video Was Shot Before She Came on His Show
articles.summary: Graham Norton has shot down a “conspiracy theory” surrounding Taylor Swift’s “Opalite” music video, in which he guest stars. Speaking at the Royal Television Society conference in London, Norton said seeing his famous “The Graham Norton Show” sofa brought to life in Swift’s video was “really odd”…
body: Broadcaster Tina Daheley, who was interviewing Norton on stage, interjected: “It was literally an idea she came up with while she was on the show.”

Norton replied: “Yeah, yeah. I don’t know, but certainly when you watch the clips, there is a moment when it looks like she’s having the idea, and it’s kind of amazing to have the show get that kind of recognition.”

The video, which was released in February this year, features Swift and Gleeson as two unlucky in love singles who eventually find their way to one another, taking part in a dance contest on the way. Lee, Turner-Smith, Murphy and Capaldi all make cameo appearances.
Swift appeared on Norton’s BBC show – which famously has an eclectic mix of celebrity guests each week — last October, appearing alongside Gleeson, Lee, Turner-Smith, Murphy and Capaldi.

articles.title: Beyond Fest Organizers on Improved Ticketing, Fans ‘As Unhinged as We Are’ and Their 7 Titles Not to Miss
articles.summary: How true is the perception that Los Angeles doesn’t have a prominent signature film festival? While the city’s film lovers were debating the question, Beyond Fest at American Cinematheque snuck in and became one of the city’s biggest and most popular cinema events, with some 37,000 people expected…
body: This year’s selection includes buzzy new releases like “Primetime” and “Musk” as well as retrospectives from “Hoffa” to “Pan’s Labyrinth,” plus under-the-radar titles that screen for free at the Los Feliz 3 cinemas, thanks to Mubi’s sponsorship.

“The inspiration was always to be more than strictly horror, back in those early years,” says co-founder Christian Parkes. “(But we also) did ‘Dog Day Afternoon.’ Our film collections and our film tastes and our DVD closets are wildly varied.”

The festival’s explosive growth trajectory coincides with young L.A. audiences’ year-round passion for attending repertory and classic film screenings since the pandemic, with Letterboxd playing a big part in stoking the interest.

“Things like Beyond Fest are a signal that things are completely changing,” says Juan Devis, president of Film Independent, the L.A.-based filmmaker organization that runs the Spirit Awards. “Young people are going back to cinema. They’re doing it because they love to do it and they do it constantly.”

articles.title: Close-up look at Turner's '£50m' Rome painting on show in the city
articles.summary: Turner’s early 19th century painting - Rome, from Mount Aventine - will be on display in the Italian capital for the first time ahead of an auction in London in December.
body: A renowned painting by British landscape artist JMW Turner has returned to the city that inspired it nearly two centuries ago.
Rome, from Mount Aventine features a panoramic view of the Italian capital and will be on display at the Palazzo Rondinini for three days.
Dating back to the 19th century, the masterpiece was based on sketches made in Rome.
The work of art is remarkably well preserved and is believed to have never been restored. It even features traces of fingerprints and brush hairs are still visible.

articles.title: The Portuguese House review – picturesque, polite drama of secrets and revelations at a country estate
articles.summary: Spanish drama about people leaving their old lives behind plays out like a literary novel, with Manolo Solo excellent as a discombobulated gardener. Out of the blue, a woman walks out on her husband.
body: Manolo Solo gives an excellent performance as the left-behind husband, Fernando, an introspective mild-mannered geography professor. After his wife’s disappearance, Fernando goes on holiday to Portugal, where he meets a gardener called Manuel. When Manuel drops dead of a heart attack, Fernando decides – like his wife – to leave his old life behind; he assumes Manuel’s identity and takes a job as the gardener at a Portuguese country estate. The owner, Amália (Maria de Medeiros), senses that this intellectual man with glasses and a clumsy way with the loppers is not the man she hired, but doesn’t push it – possibly because she is attracted to him.

Like a doorstop paperback, The Portuguese House is an expansive watch, spanning years and going at a gentle pace for nearly two hours. There are more secrets and lies to come – and another person pretending to be someone they are not. That would be a twist too far in another film, but works here in a restrained drama that treats all its characters generously and with sympathy. Though in the end I wondered if it is possibly too respectful, sweeping away difficult hard-to-shift feelings like autumn leaves.

articles.title: Sir Ranulph Fiennes' relatives tell BBC it's 'very painful' not being able to visit him
articles.summary: It has been alleged that Sir Ranulph has been admitted to a number of care homes under assumed names.
body: Relatives of the British explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes have said it is "very painful" he appears to have been hidden away from them.
Speaking to BBC Newsnight, his former sister-in-law told the BBC that she did not know where he was, and nobody had been able to see him.
Louise Millington-Cotes did not immediately respond to the allegations, or the BBC's request for comment.
Cheshire Police have said they are aware of the concerns regarding Sir Ranulph, and are satisfied he is living in an appropriate setting with suitable care.

articles.title: National museums to stay free for all visitors
articles.summary: It follows discussions about whether charging tourists could boost museums' finances.
body: Overseas visitors will not be charged to enter England's national museums after ministers decided against changing the universal free admission policy.
It comes after months of discussions between the government, museums, the tourism sector and local leaders to examine whether making tourists from abroad pay could boost the institutions' finances.
In March, the government said it would explore charging international visitors to enter national museums as it looks for ways to tackle funding pressures.
But the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) has now said this could deter domestic visitors and that any benefits of charging would not be felt equally across the sector.
